title: Lighting design for an open-plan office
subtitle: BSE3125 Optics and Lighting | First report draft for review | 16 November 2026

pages.title: Design basis and office arrangement
paragraphs: The office requires lighting for ordinary paperwork, reading and computer-based work. The design therefore adopts a maintained average illuminance of 500 lx on each desk, together with a task-area uniformity of at least 0.60 and a maximum calculated UGR of 19. These criteria are used together because sufficient average illuminance alone does not show whether individual workstations are evenly lit or comfortable to use [1,2].

The lighting arrangement follows the L-shaped office around the service core. Tracing the office-facing boundaries gives a gross floor polygon of 1042.10 m2. After deducting the eight column intersections, the usable modelled area is 1032.57 m2. The drawing also gives an area annotation of 1022 m2. As that figure differs from the traced boundary, the smaller annotated value is retained only for the conservative lighting power density calculation.

Since furniture is not specified on the supplied drawing, the proposal adopts 28 four-person benches, giving 112 desk positions. Each desk measures 1.6 by 0.8 m. This arrangement provides specific task areas for the simulation and allows the lighting to be assessed where people are expected to work. It remains a proposed office arrangement rather than an existing furniture survey.

A ceiling height of 2.8 m and a desk height of 0.8 m are adopted. Ceiling, wall and floor reflectances are assumed to be 80%, 70% and 20%, respectively, with 40% for the columns. The relatively light ceiling and walls help distribute reflected light through the office. These finishes would need to be maintained in the completed space, since darker surfaces would change the calculated lighting performance. Daylight is not included because the glazing dimensions are unavailable.

pages.title: DIALux model and calculation procedure
paragraphs: The architectural drawing was imported into DIALux evo and its scale checked against the 45 m overall building dimension. The office boundary and eight full-height columns were then represented in the model. Defining these elements before placing the luminaires allows the calculation to account for the actual room shape and the obstruction caused by the columns, rather than treating the office as an unobstructed rectangle.

Manufacturer ULD photometry was imported for the selected luminaire. This provides the angular light distribution used by DIALux to calculate direct light, while the specified surface reflectances determine the contribution of reflected light. The luminaires were positioned on complete 600 mm ceiling tiles, with their emitting faces approximately flush with the 2.8 m ceiling. Figure 2 shows the resulting room model.

Each desk was evaluated on a 1.6 by 0.8 m calculation plane at 0.8 m above the floor. A regular 10 by 5 grid gives a nominal spacing of 0.16 m. The average and minimum grid illuminances were used to calculate uniformity, Uo = Emin / Eaverage. Assessing the desks separately avoids relying on a whole-room average that could conceal a poorly lit workstation.

A maintenance factor of 0.80 was applied so that the illuminance results represent the maintained condition. Glare was calculated at a seated eye height of 1.2 m in directions spaced at 15 degrees. This checks how the installation appears from the proposed workstations; the manufacturer's catalogue UGR value is used for product selection, while the calculated room UGR is used for the design assessment [3].

Additional calculations cover the 0.5 m immediate surroundings of the bench groups, the remaining background floor, seated cylindrical illuminance and exposed wall and ceiling surfaces. The core and supplemental calculations use the same luminaire positions and photometry. Workstations are represented by evaluation planes; opaque desks, monitors and high partitions are not included in the model.

pages.title: Luminaire selection and layout
paragraphs: The proposal uses 186 Philips PowerBalance gen2 RC461B 40S/840 luminaires, order code 910505103638. Each fitting has a nominal output of 4000 lm and an input power of 23 W. The 4000 K light colour and colour rendering index above 80 are suitable for the adopted office tasks, while the manufacturer's low-glare optic makes the product a suitable candidate for workstations used for both paperwork and computer work [4].

The 597 by 597 mm body fits the 600 mm ceiling module. Coordinating the fittings with this grid gives a regular ceiling appearance and avoids placing panels across tile joints. Most of the layout uses approximately 2.4 m spacing, with local adjustments around the L-shaped boundary and columns. The resulting overlapping light distributions help illuminate the workstations between fittings, while the actual adequacy of the spacing is checked through the DIALux results.

The final output was selected after comparing the lighting level and glare performance of earlier arrangements. The refined 3400 lm PowerBalance scheme gave a minimum desk average of 504 lx, which met the target but left little allowance for variation in output. The 4000 lm version increases that minimum to 593 lx at the same positions, while the maximum calculated UGR remains below 19. It therefore provides a more useful illuminance margin without requiring a further increase in the number of fittings.

Recessed installation requires sufficient ceiling void and access for the driver and maintenance. The manufacturer's table gives an 82 mm body height, while the dimension drawing reaches 86 mm; the larger envelope should therefore be allowed, together with service clearance. The independent lighting layout on page 7 shows the ceiling grid, fixture identification, legend and luminaire schedule.

pages.title: Calculated performance and code comparison
paragraphs: All 112 proposed desks meet the adopted task illuminance, uniformity and directional glare criteria. The minimum desk average is 593 lx, the minimum uniformity is 0.80 and the maximum calculated UGR is 18.1. These are limiting values across the installation and occur at different workstations. Reporting them separately gives a clearer assessment than selecting one desk as representative of the entire office.

Desk-021 controls the average illuminance, with a mean of 593 lx and a minimum of 525 lx. Its uniformity is therefore 525/593 = 0.89. Desk-084 has the lowest uniformity, at 0.80, while Desk-018 gives the highest directional UGR, at 180 degrees. The selected native plots in the appendix show these locations. Figure 4 maps the desk averages and indicates where the lower and higher lighting levels occur.

pages.title: Lighting controls and energy use
paragraphs: The control proposal divides the office into 32 independently controlled zones, comprising 28 bench zones and four circulation zones. This allows lighting to follow the distribution of occupants rather than requiring the whole office to operate whenever one group is working. Each zone has a local manual on/off/dim interface. The largest zone is 46.67 m2, and the proposed 32 manual control points meet the unreduced BEC Table 5.5 basis for the adopted office area [5].

Occupancy control switches the light output off after 10 minutes without movement. A scheduled shutdown covers non-working periods, with a local override limited to 120 minutes for after-hours use. These settings reduce unnecessary operation while allowing staff to continue working in an occupied zone. Drivers and sensors may still draw standby power when the lights are off; the installed system should therefore be checked for the required automatic electrical-power reduction of at least 50%.

Daylight-responsive dimming is proposed where the actual facade creates qualifying daylight zones under BEC clause 5.6.2. The sensors should reduce electric light when daylight is available while maintaining the required lighting at the desks. Since window dimensions are not available, the present simulation takes no credit for daylight and does not estimate an annual energy saving.

The full-load luminaire power is 186 x 23 = 4278 W. Adding a 50 W allowance for external controls gives 4328 W, and the conservative lighting power density is 4328/1022 = 4.235 W/m2. This is below the adopted BEC office limit of 7.2 W/m2. The result indicates a relatively low connected lighting load, although actual energy consumption will also depend on occupied hours and how the controls are used.

pages.title: Discussion and conclusion
paragraphs: The design gives a useful balance between task lighting and connected power. The controlling desk average is about 19% above the adopted 500 lx target, while the other desk results remain within the assessed glare and uniformity criteria. Increasing output from the previous 3400 lm option improves the weakest task locations, although it also raises illumination elsewhere. The final scheme is therefore a satisfactory design under the stated assumptions; it has not been demonstrated to be the lowest-power arrangement that could meet the same criteria.

As a simple sensitivity check, a common 10% reduction in luminaire output would reduce the controlling 593 lx desk mean to approximately 534 lx. This gives more allowance than the earlier 504 lx design. The check is analytical and does not represent a separate simulation with unequal fixture tolerances. The maintained results also depend on the assumed finishes and maintenance factor, so the same performance should not be expected if the room is fitted with substantially darker surfaces or high partitions.

The maintenance factor of 0.80 is based on 0.90 lumen maintenance, 1.00 survival, 0.95 luminaire cleanliness and 0.94 room-surface maintenance. Their product is 0.8037, rounded down to 0.80. Annual cleaning, prompt replacement of failed units and periodic inspection of room finishes are proposed to support this assumption. Computer-screen orientation should also be reviewed after fit-out to avoid reflected images of luminaires; the calculated room UGR alone does not assess every display reflection.

Overall, the proposed lighting meets the selected task and visual-environment criteria in the DIALux model and remains below the adopted lighting power limit. Before implementation, the furniture arrangement, facade, finishes and ceiling void should be confirmed, and the controls commissioned for the actual occupancy pattern. Changes to these inputs would require a review of the calculation. The appendix contains five selected native output pages; complete results and editable engineering files are retained separately.
